title: Hangover or Food Poisoning? How to Tell the Difference
excerpt: Sick the morning after a night out? How to tell a hangover from food poisoning or a stomach bug using timing, fever, and symptoms, plus when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Hangover or food poisoning? Use timing, fever, and symptom clues to tell them apart, what to do in the first 24 hours, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a hangover and food poisoning can feel almost identical the morning after a night out, but a few clues usually separate them. A hangover starts as the alcohol leaves your system, mostly hits your head, energy, and stomach together, and steadily improves within about a day. Food poisoning tends to bring repeated vomiting or watery diarrhea, sometimes a real fever and chills, often cramping that comes in waves, and it may not ease on the same timeline. If other people who ate the same food are sick too, or you still feel awful the following day, food poisoning (or a stomach bug) becomes the more likely answer.

**The quick test:** Ask yourself four questions. Did I drink enough to explain how I feel? Do I have a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher? Am I vomiting or having diarrhea over and over, rather than once or twice? Is anyone I ate with sick too? A "no, yes, yes, yes" pattern points away from a hangover. Either way, the first-day care is mostly the same: small sips of fluid, rest, bland food when you can keep it down, and no more alcohol.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than a few hours, you see blood in your vomit or stool, you have a fever above 102°F (38.9°C), you have diarrhea lasting more than three days, you have signs of dehydration (very little or dark urine, dizziness when you stand, a racing heart, a very dry mouth), or you have severe belly pain that is constant or focused in one spot. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover, and they need emergency care. People who are pregnant, older adults, young children, and anyone with a weakened immune system should check in with a doctor sooner.

## Why a Hangover and Food Poisoning Feel So Similar

Both conditions land on the same parts of your body. Your gut is irritated, you're short on fluids, and your whole system feels inflamed and run down. That overlap is why so many people wake up after a party, a wedding, or a late-night food run and genuinely can't tell which one they have.

Here is what's going on in each case, in plain words.

**In a hangover**, alcohol has irritated the lining of your stomach and increased stomach acid. It has made you pee out more fluid than you took in, so you're mildly dehydrated. Your body has been working through acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol. Your sleep was poor even if you were in bed for hours. And your immune system has kicked up some low-level inflammation, which is part of why you feel achy and foggy. Our guide to [hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) covers each of these in more detail.

**In food poisoning**, you've swallowed a germ (a bacterium, a virus, or a parasite) or a toxin that a germ already made in the food. Your gut responds by trying to flush it out, which is where the vomiting and diarrhea come from. With some germs, your immune system mounts a full response, which brings fever, chills, and body aches.

So in both cases you get nausea, stomach upset, tiredness, a headache, and that "hit by a truck" feeling. The differences are in the timing, the type of gut symptoms, fever, and how the illness moves over the next day.

## Hangover vs Food Poisoning: Side-by-Side

| Clue | More likely a hangover | More likely food poisoning |
|---|---|---|
| When it started | As alcohol wore off, usually overnight or on waking | Anywhere from 30 minutes to several days after the bad food, depending on the germ |
| How much you drank | Enough to explain how you feel | Not much, or symptoms seem far worse than your drinking |
| Main symptoms | Headache, thirst, fatigue, light sensitivity, queasy stomach | Repeated vomiting, frequent watery diarrhea, cramping in waves |
| Fever | Usually none, or you just feel warm and clammy | A measured fever is common with some infections |
| Chills and body aches | Mild, if any | Can be prominent |
| Others affected | Only you (or only the people who drank a lot) | People who ate the same thing also get sick, including non-drinkers |
| How it changes | Improves steadily through the day, mostly gone within about 24 hours | Can come in waves and often lasts one to several days |
| Diarrhea | Possible, usually short-lived | Often frequent and the main event |
| Blood in stool or vomit | Not a normal hangover symptom | A warning sign that needs medical care |

No single clue in this table is decisive. A bad hangover can include vomiting and a loose stomach, and a mild food poisoning can feel like nothing more than a rough morning. Look at the whole picture rather than one symptom.

## Clue 1: Timing Is the Most Useful Tell

The timing of your symptoms is usually the strongest clue, because hangovers follow alcohol and food poisoning follows food.

### How hangover timing works

A hangover begins as your blood alcohol level falls back toward zero. That's why most people feel it on waking, after a night's drinking. It's typically at its worst in the morning or around midday and then fades. For most people, it's largely gone within about 24 hours, though a heavy night can leave you dragging into a second day. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains the curve in more detail.

The key pattern: **a hangover gets better, not worse, as the day goes on.** If you feel steadily better by evening, that's reassuring. If you feel worse at 6 p.m. than you did at 10 a.m., think beyond the hangover.

### How food poisoning timing works

Food poisoning is less predictable because different germs work on different clocks. Public health agencies such as the CDC describe very different onset windows depending on the cause:

- **Toxins already in the food** (from bacteria like *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Bacillus cereus*) can cause sudden vomiting within roughly 30 minutes to several hours. This is the fast, violent type that often follows food left out too long, such as a buffet, a party platter, or reheated rice.
- **Norovirus**, the common "stomach bug," usually starts about 12 to 48 hours after exposure.
- **Clostridium perfringens**, often linked to large batches of meat or gravy kept warm for hours, usually causes cramps and diarrhea within about 6 to 24 hours.
- **Salmonella** typically takes from 6 hours to several days.
- **Campylobacter** and **E. coli** infections usually take a few days to show up.

This has an important consequence: **what you ate last night is not always the cause.** If you feel sick the morning after a night out, the culprit could be the late-night tacos, but it could also be lunch from two days ago. And if you wake up feeling ordinary-hangover rough and then get much sicker the next day, the drinking and the illness may simply have overlapped.

### Putting timing together

- Felt fine at bedtime, woke up rough, improving by afternoon: **probably a hangover.**
- Sudden, forceful vomiting a few hours after eating, maybe before you'd even gone to bed, especially if friends are sick too: **think food toxin.**
- Started feeling sick a day or more after the night out, with diarrhea and maybe a fever: **think infection, such as norovirus or a bacterial food poisoning.**

## Clue 2: Fever, Chills, and Body Aches

A true fever is one of the better ways to tell these apart.

A hangover can make you feel hot, sweaty, and clammy. Your heart may run fast and you may get chills as your body readjusts. But a measured fever, generally defined as 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, is not a typical hangover symptom. Our article on [hangover fever](/never-hungover/hangover-fever) goes into why you might feel feverish without actually having one.

Many food infections, on the other hand, do cause a real fever. Salmonella, Campylobacter, and norovirus can all bring a raised temperature, chills, and muscle aches.

**What to do:** if you have a thermometer, use it. A reading of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher shifts the odds toward an infection. A fever above 102°F (38.9°C) combined with diarrhea is one of the signs the CDC lists for seeing a doctor.

One caution: toxin-type food poisoning (the fast kind from food left out too long) often causes intense vomiting *without* much fever. So no fever doesn't rule food poisoning out. It just makes certain infections less likely.

## Clue 3: The Type of Stomach Symptoms

Both conditions upset your stomach, but in different ways.

**Hangover stomach symptoms** tend to be:

- Queasiness and a sour, acidic feeling, often worse on an empty stomach
- Vomiting once or a few times, usually early in the day, and then easing
- A loose stool or two, but not hour after hour
- Heartburn or a burning feeling in the upper belly
- Gradual improvement once you get some fluid and bland food down

If this sounds familiar, our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has practical steps for settling your stomach, and [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) covers what different kinds of belly pain can mean.

**Food poisoning stomach symptoms** tend to be:

- Repeated vomiting that keeps coming back even when your stomach is empty
- Watery diarrhea many times a day, often the most noticeable symptom
- Cramping that builds and releases in waves, often followed by a trip to the bathroom
- Little improvement from eating or drinking in the first several hours

Diarrhea deserves its own note. Alcohol does speed up your gut and can cause loose stools the next day, which we explain in our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking). But hangover-related diarrhea is usually limited to a few episodes. Frequent, watery diarrhea through the day and into the night points more toward an infection.

## Clue 4: Who Else Is Sick

This is the clue people forget, and it can settle the question quickly.

- **If friends who drank as much as you feel fine** but you're the only one vomiting, and you ate something they didn't, food poisoning moves up the list.
- **If people who ate the same meal are sick, including those who didn't drink**, that strongly suggests food poisoning or a shared stomach bug.
- **If everyone who drank heavily is hurting and the non-drinkers are fine**, that's a hangover pattern.

Norovirus also spreads easily from person to person, so if someone in your group or household got sick first, you may have caught it from them rather than from food. This matters because a stomach bug can keep moving through a household, so hand-washing with soap and water and cleaning bathroom surfaces becomes important.

## Clue 5: How Much You Actually Drank

Be honest with yourself about this one. Hangovers scale roughly with how much you drank and how fast, though some people get them after fairly modest amounts.

- If you had a long night of drinking, a rough morning is expected.
- If you had two glasses of wine with dinner and woke up vomiting repeatedly with a fever, that is not a typical hangover for most people, and something else is likely going on.

That said, everyone's tolerance differs, and things like drinking on an empty stomach, poor sleep, and mixing drinks can make a hangover worse than the number of drinks suggests. Our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.

## Could It Be Both?

Yes, and it's more common than you might think. Drinking nights often go with risky eating: buffets that sat out for hours, late-night street food, undercooked burgers at a barbecue, or leftovers eaten at 2 a.m. that were left on the counter all evening. Your judgment about food safety also drops after a few drinks.

If you had both a heavy night and a questionable meal, you might get a hangover on top of a mild food poisoning. In practice, this usually looks like a morning that feels like a normal hangover but doesn't improve on schedule, or that develops diarrhea or fever later in the day.

Alcohol can also make food poisoning feel worse. It adds to dehydration, irritates the stomach lining that is already inflamed, and disrupts sleep, which your body needs to recover. So if you suspect food poisoning, stop drinking until you've fully recovered.

### Does alcohol kill food poisoning germs?

No. This is a persistent myth. The alcohol in drinks is far too diluted to sterilize your stomach or kill germs in food you've already eaten. Your stomach acid is a stronger defense than a beer or a cocktail. There is no good evidence that drinking alcohol with a meal protects you from food poisoning, and drinking while you're already sick only adds to dehydration.

### Can a hangover turn into food poisoning?

Not directly. A hangover is your body's reaction to alcohol, not an infection, and it can't turn into one. What can happen is that a food poisoning you picked up around the same time shows up after the hangover, which can make it feel like the hangover "turned into" something worse.

## Could It Be a Stomach Bug Instead?

Many people say "food poisoning" when they actually have norovirus, the stomach bug that spreads through contaminated food, surfaces, and close contact. From the inside, it feels much the same: sudden vomiting, diarrhea, cramps, sometimes a low fever and body aches.

The practical differences:

- A stomach bug often spreads through a household or group over several days, not just among people who shared one meal.
- It usually hits hard for one to three days, then improves.
- Hand sanitizer is less effective against norovirus than thorough hand-washing with soap and water.

The care at home is the same as for food poisoning. The main reason to care about the difference is to protect the people around you: wash your hands well, avoid preparing food for others while you're sick and for a couple of days after, and clean bathroom surfaces.

## Could It Be Alcohol Poisoning?

This is the most important distinction on the page, because alcohol poisoning is an emergency.

A hangover happens the *next day*, after the alcohol has mostly left your body. Alcohol poisoning happens *during or shortly after* drinking, while there is still a dangerous amount of alcohol in the blood. Signs include:

- Confusion, stupor, or being unable to wake up
- Vomiting while very drunk or barely conscious
- Slow or irregular breathing
- Seizures
- Pale or bluish skin, or a low body temperature

If you see these signs in someone, call 911. Don't let them "sleep it off," and don't leave them alone. If they're vomiting, keep them on their side so they don't choke. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to look for and what to do while you wait for help.

The overlap with food poisoning is vomiting, which is why the distinction matters. Vomiting the morning after while you're awake and alert is usually a hangover or a stomach illness. Vomiting while you're very drunk and hard to rouse is an emergency.

## What to Do in the First 24 Hours (Either Way)

The good news is that the home care for a hangover and for mild food poisoning overlaps almost completely. You don't need to know which one you have to start taking care of yourself.

### 1. Rehydrate slowly

Small, frequent sips work better than gulping a big glass, which can trigger more vomiting. Try a few sips every five to ten minutes and build up as your stomach allows. Water is fine, but if you're losing a lot of fluid through vomiting or diarrhea, an oral rehydration solution or an electrolyte drink helps replace the salts you're losing. Our [electrolyte drinks comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) covers the main options, and our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) guide works if you can't get to a store.

### 2. Rest your stomach, then start bland

Give your stomach a break while you're actively vomiting. Once you can keep fluids down, try plain, easy foods: toast, crackers, rice, bananas, applesauce, or plain broth. Avoid greasy, spicy, or very sugary food until you're feeling better. For a hangover, our [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) guide has more ideas.

### 3. Skip the alcohol

No "hair of the dog." More alcohol worsens dehydration and stomach irritation whether you're hungover or ill, and it delays recovery.

### 4. Be careful with medicines

- **Anti-diarrhea medicine** like loperamide can help some adults with mild, watery diarrhea, but the CDC and most doctors advise against using it if you have a fever or bloody stool, because in some infections it can make things worse. Check with a pharmacist if you're unsure.
- **Painkillers:** ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate an already upset stomach, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) puts extra load on the liver after heavy drinking. If you need one, use the label dose and take it with a little food. Our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide explains the liver risk.
- **Antibiotics** are not needed for most cases of food poisoning, and they don't help a hangover at all. A doctor will decide if they're appropriate.

### 5. Wash your hands

If there's any chance it's a stomach bug, wash your hands with soap and water after using the bathroom and before touching food. This helps keep it from spreading to everyone you live with.

### 6. Watch the clock

A hangover should be improving by the evening and mostly gone by the next morning. If it's not, or if you're getting worse, treat that as a sign you're dealing with something else and keep an eye on the warning signs below.

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangovers and most mild food poisoning get better at home. These are the signs that mean you should get medical care. Many of them come from CDC guidance on food poisoning.

Our guide to [severe hangover symptoms](/never-hungover/severe-hangover-symptoms) lists the warning signs that point to something more than a hangover.

**See a doctor or visit urgent care if:**

- You're vomiting so often that you can't keep liquids down for more than a few hours
- You have diarrhea that lasts more than three days
- You have a fever above 102°F (38.9°C)
- You see blood in your stool or vomit (vomit that looks like coffee grounds counts)
- You have signs of dehydration: very little urine or very dark urine, dizziness when standing, a dry mouth and throat, or a racing heart
- Your belly pain is severe, constant, or focused in one area, especially the lower right side
- You feel much worse on day two than on day one
- You're pregnant, over 65, have a weakened immune system, or have a long-term condition like diabetes or kidney disease

**Call 911 or go to an emergency room if:**

- Someone who has been drinking is confused, can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, or has a seizure
- You have signs of severe dehydration, such as fainting or confusion
- You have trouble breathing, blurred or double vision, trouble swallowing, or muscle weakness, which can be signs of rare but serious food-borne illnesses like botulism

**A note for people who drink every day.** If you drink heavily most days and you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or sick when you stop, that may be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover or food poisoning. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so tell a doctor plainly about your drinking and get checked rather than trying to tough it out at home.

## Can You Drink Alcohol After Food Poisoning?

It's best to wait until you're fully recovered: eating normally, keeping fluids down, and no longer having diarrhea. For many people that's a day or two after symptoms end, but there's no fixed rule. Your stomach lining may stay sensitive for a few days, and alcohol can bring back nausea and loose stools. When you do drink again, start light, eat first, and drink water alongside.

If you were prescribed antibiotics for a food-borne infection, ask the pharmacist about alcohol. Some antibiotics, such as metronidazole, have a well-known reaction with alcohol. Our guide on [how long after antibiotics you can drink](/never-hungover/how-long-after-antibiotics-can-you-drink) covers the common ones.

## How to Lower the Odds of Both Next Time

You can't completely prevent either, but a few habits help with both.

**For food poisoning:**

- Be wary of food that has been sitting out for more than about two hours, or one hour on a hot day. Party platters and buffets are common culprits.
- Make sure meat, chicken, and eggs are cooked through.
- Refrigerate leftovers promptly, and think twice about eating something that sat out all night.
- Wash your hands before eating, especially at events.

**For hangovers:**

- Eat a real meal before you drink.
- Pace yourself, and alternate alcoholic drinks with water.
- Stop drinking a few hours before bed so your body has time to clear some of the alcohol.
- Know your limit and stick to it. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Let's be clear: **no supplement treats food poisoning or a stomach bug.** If you suspect food poisoning, focus on fluids, rest, and the warning signs above.

For hangovers specifically, some people add DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, to their routine before or while drinking. Lab and animal studies suggest it may help the body process alcohol and its by-products, but human research is still limited, and there is no good evidence that it prevents every hangover or that it does anything for an upset stomach caused by food. It's an optional extra, not a replacement for pacing yourself and eating.

If you want to try it, two options we've reviewed are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **Timing is your best clue.** Hangovers start as alcohol wears off and improve through the day. Food poisoning can start anywhere from 30 minutes to several days after the food, depending on the cause.
- **A measured fever** of 100.4°F (38°C) or more, frequent watery diarrhea, and vomiting that keeps coming back all point more toward food poisoning or a stomach bug.
- **Other people matter.** If non-drinkers who shared your meal are sick, it's probably not a hangover.
- **The first-day care is the same:** small sips of fluid with electrolytes, bland food when you can, rest, and no more alcohol.
- **Know the red flags:** blood in vomit or stool, a high fever, no fluids staying down, signs of dehydration, or symptoms getting worse instead of better mean it's time to see a doctor. Confusion, slow breathing, or someone who can't be woken after drinking means call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How can I tell if I have a hangover or food poisoning?**

Look at timing, fever, the type of stomach symptoms, and who else is sick. A hangover starts as alcohol wears off, usually on waking, and improves through the day. Food poisoning often brings repeated vomiting, frequent watery diarrhea, cramping in waves, and sometimes a measured fever. If people who ate the same food are sick too, including non-drinkers, food poisoning is more likely.

**Can a hangover cause a fever?**

A hangover can make you feel hot, sweaty, and shivery, but a measured fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is not a typical hangover symptom. If a thermometer shows a real fever, an infection such as food poisoning or a stomach bug is more likely. A fever above 102°F (38.9°C) with diarrhea is a reason to see a doctor.

**How soon after eating does food poisoning start?**

It depends on the cause. Toxins already in food can cause vomiting within about 30 minutes to several hours. Norovirus usually starts 12 to 48 hours after exposure, and some bacteria, such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, and E. coli, can take a day to several days. That means the food that made you sick isn't always the last thing you ate.

**How long does a hangover last compared with food poisoning?**

Most hangovers are largely gone within about 24 hours and improve steadily as the day goes on. Mild food poisoning usually lasts one to a few days, and it can come in waves rather than improving smoothly. If you feel worse in the evening than in the morning, or you're still sick the next day, something other than a hangover is likely involved.

**Can you have a hangover and food poisoning at the same time?**

Yes. Drinking nights often involve risky food, like buffets that sat out, late-night takeout, or leftovers left on the counter. If you have both, it often looks like a hangover that doesn't improve on schedule or that develops diarrhea or fever later in the day. Stop drinking, focus on fluids and electrolytes, and watch for warning signs.

**Does drinking alcohol kill food poisoning bacteria?**

No. The alcohol in drinks is far too diluted to kill germs in your stomach or in food you've eaten. There is no good evidence that drinking with a meal protects you from food poisoning, and drinking while you're sick adds to dehydration and stomach irritation.

**Should I take anti-diarrhea medicine for food poisoning after drinking?**

For mild, watery diarrhea without fever, loperamide can help some adults. Avoid it if you have a fever or blood in your stool, because in some infections it can make things worse. Focus on replacing fluids and electrolytes first, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure what's safe with your other medicines.

**When should I go to the doctor for vomiting after drinking?**

Get medical care if you can't keep fluids down for more than a few hours, see blood in your vomit or stool, have a fever above 102°F, have diarrhea for more than three days, or show signs of dehydration like dark or very little urine and dizziness. Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't be woken, has slow or irregular breathing, or has a seizure, because that can be alcohol poisoning.
